extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Plato, classical literature, and aesthetics; readers studying the Republic and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the evaluative principles used by Plato (as explained by the commentator) for judging poetry and the imitative arts—criteria about truth, knowledge, morality, usefulness, and political effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation: poetry thrice removed from truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic poet is an imitator, and, like every other imitator, is thrice removed from the king and from the truth; the painter imitates the carpenter’s bed and so is twice/thrice removed from the absolute idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via the three beds (God’s ideal bed, the carpenter’s bed, the painter’s image). Anti-pattern: treating poetic representations as equivalent to philosophical or factual truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets lack true knowledge of their subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitator has no knowledge of reality, but only of appearance; he can represent an art without possessing that art’s expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a painter can paint a cobbler without being able to cobble; the poet delineates arts in the 'colours of language' without true technical understanding. Scoring note: works that display demonstrable expert knowledge count higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art appeals to inferior parts of the soul (emotion over reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is concerned with an inferior part of the soul; he indulges the feelings while he enfeebles the reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work stimulates rational reflection (higher faculties) or primarily stirs appetite/passion (lower faculties). Anti-patterns: art that substitutes feeling for judgment or undermines reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry injuriously excites feelings and encourages moral weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry has the power of injuriously exciting the feelings—sympathizing with others’ laments may encourage self-indulgence; comedy may teach buffoonery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess emotional effects: does the work promote imprudent indulgence (negative) or controlled catharsis/consolation (potentially positive)? Examples: long heroic lamentations, coarse stage merriment as harmful influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness over mere delight (utility requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry must show that it is useful as well as delightful; otherwise it should be renounced despite its charms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted exceptions are narrow (e.g., hymns to the gods, praise of famous men). Criterion: does the work educate or improve the soul (preferred) rather than only entertain?

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must be subject to rule and measure
rubrics_metrics.description: His creations are not tested by rule and measure; they are only appearances—unregulated imitation lacks the discipline of measured, rule-governed inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for works that conform to recognized standards/techniques or that can be evaluated against principles (versus purely deceptive or rhetorical flourish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting/multiple roles risk personal degradation
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession of an actor was regarded as a degradation: 'one man in his life cannot play many parts'—the characters an actor performs seem to destroy his own character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating dramatic practice, consider whether role-playing undermines moral or psychological integrity of performers or culture; used as basis for stronger sanctions against dramatic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether art harmonizes or enervates the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts might have the effect of harmonizing as well as of enervating the mind; they can console and elevate as well as weaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance Plato’s strictures by assessing positive effects (e.g., consolation through music, sublimity in architecture, elevation by nature). Works that harmonize and strengthen reason are more defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political alignment and social consequences (poets as apologists for tyranny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets are often friends of the tyrant and bask in patronage; literature corrupted by rulers can serve despotism and mislead the masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the political consequences of a work: does it praise or legitimize unjust power? Anti-pattern: literature serving as propaganda for tyrants or false teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness: universals versus particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato values universals (ideas) as the truly real; he criticizes poets for focusing on particulars of sense which are removed from universals and thus (in his view) from truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Aristotle’s view (poetry concerned with universals). Criterion: does the work express general truths/insights (more valuable on some views) or merely particulars of appearance?

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity of art to ennoble low subjects or embody the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Though Plato objects, the commentator admits an artist may ennoble humble subjects (Rembrandt, Turner) or embody the divine (Pheidias)—so some art transcends mere imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize exceptional works that impart dignity/ideal interest to ordinary things; such works are counted as nearer to truth and value despite Plato’s general objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets are unreliable interpreters of their own work
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one was a better interpreter of their writings than they were themselves; poets cease to be authoritative interpreters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning interpretative weight, prioritize critical/theoretical analysis over authorial intent; treat poets’ self-claims skeptically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational purpose: art should aid formation of moral choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole of education should be directed to acquiring knowledge that teaches a man to refuse evil and choose the good; art should assist this capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by their contribution to moral education—do they prepare readers to resist temptation and choose the mean? Use the tale of Er as a pedagogical exemplar of choosing rightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as potential corrupter versus revealer of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets are often representatives of falsehood and feigning—'false priests, false prophets, lying spirits'—and thus can corrupt belief; yet some art can reveal higher truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh whether a work disseminates false beliefs and emotional manipulation (negative) versus whether it discloses genuine insight or elevates understanding (positive).
